title: Children, Not Slaves: Hagar and Sarah
sum: Paul has argued that the law was a guardian until Christ came (3:23-25). Chapter 4 opens with a picture of an heir who is still a minor and so is no better off than a slave. God sent his Son and then the Spirit of his Son, so that the Galatians, Gentiles who once served gods that are not gods, are now sons and heirs and can call God 'Abba, Father.' Then Paul asks why they want to go back to 'weak and poor elements' by watching days and months (4:8-11).

The second half turns personal. Paul reminds them how they welcomed him when he was sick (4:12-20), then asks the people who want to live under the law to listen to the law: Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman (4:21-31). He reads the story as an allegory of two covenants and two Jerusalems. It is one of the most debated passages in the New Testament, and it has been used both well and badly.
readings: Read as an argument about Gentiles

Everything in this chapter is addressed to Gentile believers who are being told they must become Jews to belong (4:8; 4:21). On this reading, Paul is not describing what the Torah means for Jews. He is saying what it would mean for Gentiles who take it up as a condition for belonging to Abraham's family. The harsh words about 'slavery' fit that situation (a reading of scholars who place Paul within Judaism).
Read as Paul's contrast of two ages

Another reading takes the 'we' of 4:3-5 as including Jews and Gentiles alike. Before Christ the whole world, Jew and Gentile, was under the powers (the 'elements'), and the Torah, though holy, was held in that age's captivity. Christ and the Spirit begin a new age. The Hagar story then describes the old age and the new.
Read through its history of use

The pairing of Hagar with the Old Covenant and Sarah with the Church was common in Christian teaching for centuries (the Orthodox card below shows it in Chrysostom), and the passage was often heard as saying that the Jewish people are Hagar's children, under slavery and cast out. That reading is not in Paul's text, where those 'under the law' are the people who want the Galatians to be circumcised (4:21). It fed anti-Jewish teaching; this page does not catalogue particular cases. Many scholars and churches now read the passage against that history.

views.H: The Galatians were Gentiles who had served local gods (4:8), and some of the festivals and months of 4:10 may have been pagan rather than Jewish. Heirs under guardians were a familiar sight in Roman provinces, though the exact law Paul has in mind is debated. 'Arabia' in 4:25 would have meant the Nabataean kingdom east and south of Judea. The scene in 4:13-15 (the sick visitor, the welcome 'like an angel') suits the Lystra story in Acts 14 if the Galatians were the South Galatian churches, but it fits the North Galatian view too. The date of the letter depends on the view: before the Jerusalem meeting of Acts 15 (South Galatian, about AD 48-49) or in the mid-50s from Ephesus (North Galatian). See the book's opening pages.
views.C: Textual variants matter at 4:6 ('our' or 'your' hearts), 4:7, 4:14, 4:15, 4:19, 4:25 (is 'Hagar' original?), 4:26 and 4:28. Scholars see 4:4-6 as built on a traditional formula, 'God sent his Son ... God sent the Spirit of his Son' (compare Romans 8:3, 15). The rhetorical genre of the letter is debated. Whatever its genre, 4:12-20 is a personal appeal of the kind letter writers made between arguments. Because the opponents never speak in the letter, anything said about their teaching ('mirror reading', 4:17) is a reconstruction. The 'elements of the world' (4:3, 9) have at least five main readings.
views.L: The chapter has four parts. An illustration (4:1-7) comes first. A rebuke follows (4:8-11), then a warm appeal (4:12-20, with its shift of tone that Paul himself mentions in 4:20), then an Old Testament argument (4:21-31) that ends with a quotation of Isaiah 54:1 and an order from Genesis 21:10. Pronouns move: 'we' (4:3-5), 'you' (4:6-7), 'I' and 'you' (4:12-20), 'we' again (4:26, 28, 31). Pairs of opposites carry the allegory: slave and free, flesh and Spirit, now and above, Sinai and promise. The key word 'slave' runs through the chapter (4:1, 3, 7, 8, 9, 22-31).
views.J: Paul's Genesis reading belongs to a time when Jewish teachers read the Torah closely for hidden meaning. Philo made Hagar 'preliminary studies' and Sarah wisdom, and the rabbis read Ishmael's 'laughing' as sexual immorality, idolatry or bloodshed (Genesis Rabbah 53:11). Paul's method is of that kind, though his conclusion is his own. Jewish readers have objected that the allegory makes the Sinai covenant a place of slavery, which no Jewish teacher would say. Scholars who read Paul within Judaism reply that the 'slavery' belongs to a particular use of the law by Gentiles; they note that Paul himself says the law is holy (Romans 7:12) and Israel's gifts are not taken back (Romans 11:29). 'Born under the law' (4:4) is Paul's own statement that Jesus lived as a Jew.
views.T: Chrysostom explained that Paul calls a 'type' an allegory. Aquinas used the passage for the 'allegorical sense' of Scripture. Luther (lectures of 1535) set Hagar's side in the home of the Law and Sarah's in the spiritual Jerusalem of the promise. Calvin said Paul's 'allegory' is a comparison, not a hunt for hidden meaning. See the cards.

deep.h: Hagar and Sarah, step by step
deep.b:
Paul sets out the allegory in two columns, which is what the verb systoichei ('lines up with') suggests:

  • Hagar: the slave woman; the son born in the way of the flesh; the covenant from Mount Sinai in Arabia; the present Jerusalem; slavery; the child who persecutes.
  • Sarah: the free woman; the son born by the promise; the other covenant, the promise to Abraham; the Jerusalem above; freedom; 'our mother'; Isaiah's barren woman who has many children.

Notice that Paul makes Hagar stand for Sinai and the present Jerusalem, and not the Jewish people as such. The two women are in the story of Abraham's household; the two Jerusalems are in the city of Paul's day. The thing that joins them is a way of belonging to Abraham's family: by human effort and descent, or by God's promise. The Gentile Galatians, Paul argues, are already Isaac's kind of child. They do not need to take on Ishmael's mark to belong.

Paul does not say what happens to the other side. The only instruction is 'Throw out the slave woman and her son' (4:30), which some scholars take as a command to expel the agitators. It is not a statement about Jews. Romans 9:6-9 uses the same Isaac and Ishmael story differently, and Romans 11 ends with the hope that 'all Israel will be saved'.

deep.h: Hagar in Jewish, Christian and Muslim memory
deep.b: Hagar is a figure whom three faiths remember. In the Bible she is the first person to give God a name ('the God who sees me', Genesis 16:13), and the only woman in Genesis to whom a messenger of God promises a nation (Genesis 16:10; 21:18). Genesis Rabbah 45:1 gives Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's view that she was a daughter of Pharaoh, given to Abraham's house as a servant. In Islamic tradition Hagar (Hajar) is Ishmael's mother and a model of trust in God, and the pilgrim's run between Safa and Marwa during the Hajj remembers her search for water. Phyllis Trible and Letty Russell collected readings from the three traditions, and Delores Williams read Hagar as a figure for African American women who were made to survive in the wilderness, a reading that asks what Paul's story leaves out. Paul's allegory has one purpose and does not tell Hagar's whole story.

deep.title: Spec: the pronoun that slips at 4:6
deep.b: Claude's theory, offered as a suggestion. In 4:6 Paul says 'because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts.' The change from 'you' to 'our' is odd, and some manuscripts smooth it to 'your'. I suggest the slip is deliberate: Paul includes himself and other Jewish believers beside the Gentile 'you', so that the Spirit's cry of 'Abba' is the shared proof that Jew and Gentile have one status. That would match the shifts between 'we' and 'you' in 3:23-4:7, where the 'we' under the law (Jews) and the 'you' who were enslaved to the elements (Gentiles) meet in one family. This is my own suggestion; I am not citing published work for it. It would fail if 'our' is a scribal slip, or if Paul uses 'we' loosely for everyone.

echoes: Genesis 15:1-6; Genesis 16; Genesis 17:15-21; Genesis 21:8-21; Exodus 3:1; Exodus 19:1-3; Isaiah 51:1-3; Isaiah 54:1-3; Psalm 87:5; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Romans 4:17-21; Romans 8:14-17; Romans 9:6-9; 2 Corinthians 3:6-18; Colossians 2:16-20; Hebrews 12:22; Mark 14:36

settings.what: The heir under guardians, and the warning against going back
settings.to: The Gentile believers in the churches of Galatia, who once served gods that are 'no gods' (4:8), now urged to take on circumcision and the Jewish calendar
settings.when: after Paul heard that the Galatians were turning to another gospel (1:6), probably in the late 40s or the 50s AD (the date depends on where the churches were)
settings.why: to show the Galatians that they already have the status they are being urged to earn. The heir who is a minor, the sending of the Son and the Spirit, and the cry of 'Abba' all say that they are sons and heirs, not slaves. Taking up the law's observances (days, months, seasons, years) as a condition of belonging would put them back under the 'elements'.
settings.readers: Gentile Christ-followers for whom the Jewish festivals and circumcision were new and attractive. Ordinary hearers of the letter in the assembly would catch the household picture at once, since guardians and inheritance were everyday matters.
views: The readers are the churches of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13-14), founded on Paul's first journey.
The readers are the Celtic-descended people of the north-central highlands near Ankara, reached on Paul's later journey (Acts 16:6; 18:23).

settings.to: The same Galatian believers, now as friends he had once been welcomed by
settings.when: in the middle of the letter, after the argument of chapters 3-4 and before the Hagar and Sarah story
settings.why: to bring the argument down to a personal level. Paul recalls how the Galatians took him in when he was ill, asks where that goodwill has gone, warns that the agitators are courting them for their own purpose, and says he is in labor for them again. The aim is to win them back by affection, not just by argument.
settings.readers: A mixed group of Gentile believers who had treated Paul with great kindness and now saw him as an enemy. The warmth was meant to remind them of what they had received.

settings.what: The allegory of Hagar and Sarah
settings.to: 'You who want to be under the law': the Galatian Gentiles who were considering circumcision
settings.when: as the last argument from Scripture, after the appeal of 4:12-20
settings.why: to answer the agitators' use of the Abraham story with Abraham's own household. Paul argues that those who are children of the promise, as Isaac was, are free, and that the agitators' way leads to slavery. The story ends with a command to the community (4:30) and a statement of identity: 'we are not the slave woman's children, but the free woman's.'
settings.readers: People who knew Genesis from hearing it read, probably in the synagogue or from the agitators themselves. Many had met Abraham first through the agitators' account of him, so Paul's version asked them to hear the same text again.
views: The allegory is aimed at a use of Genesis 17 that the agitators made (a view some scholars hold): Gentiles, they said, must become Abraham's children by circumcision, as Ishmael and the slaves of his household had.
Paul argues from his own gospel
The allegory is Paul's own and not an answer to anything the agitators said; it illustrates what 3:6-29 has already argued (a view some scholars hold).

traditions.q: Does 'born of a woman' (4:4) say anything about the virgin birth?
views: The Catechism opens its account of Christ's coming with Galatians 4:4: 'God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law' (422). Citing 'God sent forth his Son', it says God chose for the mother of his Son 'a daughter of Israel, a young Jewish woman of Nazareth' and speaks of 'a virgin betrothed' (488).
Chrysostom takes 'born of a woman, under the Law' (4:4-5) as stating two effects of the Incarnation: deliverance from the curse of the Law, and promotion to sonship.

Luther's lectures of 1535 read 'born of a woman' as showing that Christ was born a true man, and add: 'That he has a virgin in mind is obvious.' The Augsburg Confession (art. III) says Christ 'was born of the Virgin Mary'.

Calvin reads 'made of a woman' as the Son taking our nature, so that he has two natures, and as showing that he was formed of his mother's substance and not by ordinary generation. The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 35) cites Galatians 4:4 with Matthew 1 and John 1:14 for the Son taking a human nature from the virgin Mary, and the Westminster Confession (8.2) says he was 'conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, in the womb of the virgin Mary'.
The Thirty-Nine Articles (Article II) say the Word 'took Man's nature in the womb of the blessed Virgin, of her substance'.
The Baptist Faith and Message (art. II) says Jesus was 'conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary'.

traditions.q: Does Paul's rebuke about 'days, months, seasons and years' (4:10) reach the weekly Sabbath?
views: Seventh-day Adventists keep the seventh-day Sabbath. Their Fundamental Belief 20 says God established it at Creation for all people, as a memorial of Creation, to be kept as a day of rest, worship and ministry.

The Westminster Confession (21.7-8) teaches that one day in seven is set apart by God's moral law, now the Lord's Day on the first day. Calvin took Paul's words to condemn keeping days as a requirement for justification or as superstition, not the church's choice of days for worship.

The Catechism says Sunday 'is expressly distinguished from the sabbath which it follows chronologically every week; for Christians its ceremonial observance replaces that of the sabbath' (2175), and that Sunday worship 'fulfills the moral command of the Old Covenant' (2176).
Chrysostom reads 4:10 as showing that the Galatians' teachers were preaching 'not only circumcision, but also the feast-days and new-moons'.
No day is holy in itself. The Augsburg Confession (art. 28) and Luther's Large Catechism keep Sunday for the sake of order and the hearing of the Word, and as Christian freedom, not as a law.
The Baptist Faith and Message (art. VIII) begins: 'The first day of the week is the Lord's Day.'

The Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations says Messianic Judaism seeks 'to fulfill Israel's covenantal responsibility embodied in the Torah within a New Covenant context', and that Jewish observance there 'draws upon Jewish tradition'. Its statement does not name Sabbath or festivals and does not comment on Galatians 4:10, so a reader must ask how this framework meets Paul's words to Gentiles about 'days, months, seasons and years'.

traditions.q: What is the Hagar and Sarah story about, and who are Hagar's children?
views: Aquinas used the passage to explain the four senses of Scripture, the allegorical sense among them. The Catechism says 'the Old Covenant has never been revoked' (121) and quotes Paul that 'the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable' (839), and Nostra Aetate 4 says the Jews 'should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures'.

Chrysostom explains that Paul calls a type an allegory: the history 'not only declares that which appears on the face of it, but announces somewhat farther'. He takes Hagar and Sarah as 'two covenants, two laws', and Hagar's side as the Old Covenant given at Sinai.
Luther (1535) puts Hagar's side in 'the home of the Law, the Temple, the priesthood, the ceremonies', and says Sarah stands for 'that spiritual Jerusalem where there is no Law but only the promise'.

Calvin said Paul's 'allegory' is a comparison drawn from the history itself, and that the mystical sense was 'not inconsistent with the true and literal meaning'. The Westminster Confession (7.5-6) holds that the covenant of grace was 'differently administered' under the law and under the gospel, but that there are not two covenants of grace 'differing in substance, but one and the same, under various dispensations'.

Article VII of the Thirty-Nine Articles says the Old Testament 'is not contrary to the New'. Lightfoot, an Anglican bishop, held that in Paul's hands Hagar's career is an allegory 'because it is a history': 'the symbol and the thing symbolized are the same in kind'.

title: Free to Love: Flesh and Spirit
sum: Chapter 5 opens with the letter's sharpest warning. Christ freed the Galatians for freedom, so they must not take up a slave's yoke again (5:1). If they let themselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no use to them and they owe the whole law (5:2-4). What counts in Christ is neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, but 'faith working through love' (5:6). Paul is confident that the person who is disturbing them will pay for it, and he wishes the agitators would go the whole way and castrate themselves (5:12).

Then the tone changes. Freedom is not a launching point for the flesh but a call to serve one another in love, and love fulfills the whole law (5:13-15). The rest of the chapter is about two powers, the flesh and the Spirit, and the lives they produce: the works of the flesh, and the fruit of the Spirit (5:16-26). The Galatians are not left to fight the flesh with rules. They are told to walk by the Spirit, who is leading them already.
readings: Read as the end of the argument about the law

Chapter 5 gathers what chapters 3-4 argued. Gentile believers need not and should not be circumcised, because the Spirit and faith already give what circumcision was said to give, and because circumcision is the first step toward a whole system. This is the common reading.
Read as ethics for a quarreling church

The community was already biting and devouring one another (5:15) and competing (5:26). On this reading the vice and virtue lists are not general moral advice but a mirror held up to the Galatian assemblies, which had split over the circumcision question.
Read through the believer's inner battle

Many readers hear in 5:17 the believer's divided will, as in Romans 7:15-25. Others hear a contrast of two ages or two powers, not an inner debate, so that those led by the Spirit are already free of the flesh's rule (5:18, 24). Reformation and Holiness traditions took the verse different ways; see the card.

views.H: In the first century a Gentile man who wanted to join Israel was circumcised. Whether God-fearers who stayed uncircumcised could be saved was argued among Jews (Josephus tells of the royal convert Izates and his two teachers). Gentile Christ-followers were in an awkward position: they were not Jews, and they were no longer worshipping the local gods. Circumcision looked like a way to get a recognized place. The Galatians would also have known the castrated priests of Cybele, whom 5:12 may recall.
views.C: The textual issues are at 5:1 (a differently built sentence in the Byzantine text), 5:19 (adultery in the KJV list) and 5:21 (murders). The agitators are known only from Paul's replies, and scholars have named them in at least five ways (see 5:10). The 'works of the law' of 2:16 and 3:2 return as 'the whole law' (5:3). Notice the verbal links to Romans: 'led by the Spirit' (5:18; Romans 8:14), 'the flesh desires against the Spirit' (5:17; Romans 7-8), love as the fulfilling of the law (5:14; Romans 13:8-10).
views.L: Three movements: a warning (5:1-12), a call to love and freedom (5:13-15), and the Spirit against the flesh (5:16-26). The chapter is full of contrasts: slavery and freedom (5:1, 13), the flesh and the Spirit (5:16-25), works and fruit (5:19-22), law and Spirit (5:18, 23). The sentence 'faith working through love' (5:6) is the center, answered by 'serve one another through love' (5:13) and by 'love' first in the list of the Spirit's fruit (5:22). Paul's humor and his anger come together in 5:12.
views.J: Jewish readers will notice that Paul's warning is addressed to Gentiles and says nothing against Jewish circumcision. The statement that a circumcised man owes the whole law (5:3) is a fair account of what conversion to Judaism meant. Paul's 'walk by the Spirit' (5:16) is a kind of halakhah, a way of life, for Gentile followers of the Messiah. The summary of the law in Leviticus 19:18 (5:14) was shared with Akiva and Hillel. Scholars who read Paul within Judaism say Paul did not oppose circumcision for Jews, and they take 5:11 (the charge that he preached circumcision) to show that.
views.T: Chrysostom reads 5:2 as a threat: a man who is circumcised 'for fear of the Law' distrusts the power of grace. Calvin read 5:4 as a warning against mixing the works of the law with Christ. Chrysostom took the 'flesh' of 5:17 to be the depraved will and not the body; Luther told those who feel the flesh fighting the Spirit not to despair; Wesley's sermon 'On Sin in Believers' holds that the flesh remains in the newly born (see the card). The churches answer 'Can a believer fall from grace?' (5:4) in different ways; see the cards.

deep.h: Why would Gentiles want to be circumcised, and who said they should?
deep.b:
Genesis 17:9-14 makes circumcision the sign of Abraham's covenant for his household and for every male 'bought with money from any foreigner'. So a Gentile who wanted to be counted among Abraham's descendants had a clear path: circumcision, immersion and sacrifice, and a promise to keep the Torah. By Paul's time some Jews also taught that righteous Gentiles would have a share in the world to come (a teaching later written in the Tosefta, Sanhedrin 13), and many Gentiles attached themselves to synagogues as 'God-fearers' without converting.

The Galatian Gentiles were in a new position: they trusted a Jewish Messiah, they met in their own assemblies, and the agitators told them that unless they were circumcised, they were only guests. Josephus' story of Izates (Antiquities 20.34-48) shows that Jewish teachers disagreed: one told the king he could keep the Torah without circumcision, another said he must be circumcised or he was breaking the law. On the usual reading the agitators sided with the second (the letter gives only Paul's side). For Gentile believers, the offer had a practical side too: a recognized status in the Jewish community.

Paul does not argue that circumcision is wrong. He says it is not needed for Gentiles, and that to add it is to hold that Christ's work is not enough (5:2-4). Nor does he say Jews should stop. See 5:11 and 6:12-13.

deep.h: Flesh and Spirit: the two powers
deep.b:
Chapter 5 has a pair of powers that fight over the believer: the flesh (sarx) and the Spirit (pneuma). Paul uses 'flesh' for the human way of life apart from God, and the works that come from it are named (5:19-21). The Spirit is God's gift, and the fruit it grows is named (5:22-23). The picture owes something to the Jewish teaching of two spirits and two inclinations. The Qumran Community Rule has a teaching of two spirits, of truth and of falsehood, with a list of the ways of each, and the rabbis spoke of a good and an evil inclination (yetzer). Paul's difference is that the Spirit is not a human faculty but God's own presence.

Romans 7-8 uses the same language, but the setting differs. In Romans the sharp conflict comes under the law (Romans 7), and the Spirit brings release (Romans 8). In Galatians the Spirit is already leading the community, and the flesh is the force that shows up in their quarrels. The verb 'crucified' in 5:24 is in the past; the flesh has been dealt with, though its passions still make themselves felt.

deep.title: Spec: why the fruit is singular
deep.b: Claude's theory, offered as a suggestion. Paul writes 'the fruit of the Spirit is' (singular) and then lists nine. Many readers say the one fruit is love and the other eight are its faces. My suggestion is that the singular does the same work as 5:6 and 5:13-14: faith, love and the Spirit make one life, and the list describes what that one life looks like in a community that is tearing itself apart (5:15, 26). If so, 'joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control' answer the vices of 5:20-21 one by one: peace against hatreds and strife, patience against anger, kindness against jealousy and envy, gentleness against factions and selfish ambition. This is my own suggestion; I am not citing published work for it. It would fail if the list was borrowed whole from a stock of Greek virtues with no link to the quarrel.

echoes: Genesis 17:9-14; Leviticus 18:5; Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 23:1; Deuteronomy 27:26; Psalm 119; Isaiah 54:1; Matthew 11:28-30; Matthew 22:37-40; Mark 12:28-31; Acts 15:1-11; Acts 16:3; Romans 6:14; Romans 7:7-25; Romans 8:1-17; Romans 13:8-14; 1 Corinthians 5:6; 1 Corinthians 6:9-11; Colossians 3:5-14; James 2:8-10

settings.to: The Gentile believers in the Galatian assemblies who were being urged to be circumcised
settings.when: as the practical conclusion of the argument of chapters 3-4
settings.why: to tell the Galatians that they must choose. Paul, on his own authority ('I, Paul'), says that taking circumcision on themselves would make Christ useless to them, would put them under the whole law, and would cut them off from grace. He reminds them how well they began and says the persuasion does not come from God. He ends by describing the agitators' fate and his own persecution as proof that he has not changed his message.
settings.readers: Gentile men and their households, who had to decide whether to be circumcised. The warning was blunt because the decision was close.
views: The warning is for all Christians
Paul is stating a rule that applies to anyone who seeks to be justified by law.
Paul speaks only to Gentile believers, and says nothing against Jewish circumcision, which he assumes continues (a view of scholars who read Paul within Judaism).

settings.what: Freedom for service and the summary of the law
settings.to: The same Galatian assemblies, now seen as communities in quarrel (5:15)
settings.when: after the warning against circumcision and before the call to walk by the Spirit
settings.why: to stop the Galatians from hearing 'freedom' as permission to do anything. Freedom is for service, and the whole law, which the agitators urged on them, is summed up in the one command of Leviticus 19:18. If the Galatians live by that command they do not need circumcision to be doing what the law was for.
settings.readers: People whom the conflict had made hostile toward each other, who needed to be told that the point of freedom was to love.

settings.what: Walking by the Spirit, and the two lists
settings.to: The Galatian believers, in a community with rivalries and factions
settings.when: as the positive answer to the question 'if not the law, what keeps us from the flesh?'
settings.why: to show that the Spirit, and not the law, is what guards the community against the flesh. The list of works of the flesh names the sins that threaten them, and the list of the Spirit's fruit names the character they should show. The final lines turn the lists back on the Galatians: since we live by the Spirit, let us fall in line with the Spirit and not challenge and envy one another.
settings.readers: People who had asked whether the law was needed to keep order; Paul's answer is that the Spirit does it better and that the law has nothing to say against the Spirit's fruit.

traditions.q: Can a believer fall away from grace (5:4)?
views: Yes. Grace is lost by mortal sin, though faith may remain, and a person who has fallen can rise again, through the sacrament of penance (Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 15 and canons 28-29; Catechism 1861).
Chrysostom, writing of the Galatians' loss of what they had received, says they 'had fallen from grace; nevertheless ... if ye have the purpose, ye may recover yourselves' (on Galatians 3:4).

Believers can lose the Holy Spirit by sin, and can be restored whenever they repent: the Augsburg Confession (art. XII) condemns those who deny that the justified can lose the Holy Ghost, and those who refuse absolution to the repentant.

No. The Westminster Confession (17) says those whom God has accepted 'can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace'; the Canons of Dort (fifth head) teach the perseverance of the saints. Calvin read Paul's words as a warning against mixing the works of the law with Christ: 'the smallest part of justification cannot be attributed to the law without renouncing Christ and his grace.'
Yes. Article XVI of the Thirty-Nine Articles says that after receiving the Holy Spirit we may depart from grace given and fall into sin, and by the grace of God rise again and amend our lives.

Yes. The Methodist Articles of Religion (Article XII) say that after receiving the Holy Ghost we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin, and, by the grace of God, rise again and amend our lives.

The Baptist Faith and Message (art. V) says 'All true believers endure to the end', and the 1689 Baptist Confession (ch. 17) says true saints 'can neither totally nor finally fall from the state of grace'.

traditions.q: Does the believer still carry a flesh that fights the Spirit (5:16-17), and can that fight end in this life?
views: The inclination to sin (concupiscence) remains in the baptized for the struggle, but is not itself sin (Council of Trent, session 5; Catechism 1264, 2515-2516). The Spirit gives strength to resist and to grow in holiness.

Chrysostom says that when Paul writes 'the flesh lusteth against the Spirit' he does not mean the body: 'he is wont to call the flesh, not the natural body but the depraved will', 'the earthly mind, slothful and careless'.

Luther told readers who feel the flesh battling the Spirit not to despair: 'Martin, you will never be without sin, for you have flesh. Despair not, but resist the flesh.' He added that 'the better Christian a man is, the more he will experience the heat of the conflict.'

Sanctification is real but incomplete in this life: some remnants of corruption remain in every part of the person, and from them comes a continual and irreconcilable war between the flesh and the Spirit (Westminster Confession 13.2).

Wesley's sermon 'On Sin in Believers' teaches that sin remains in those who are born anew: he quotes the Ninth Article that 'this infection of nature doth remain, yea, in them that are regenerated'. It also says that the believer's heart is 'purified by faith'.

Holiness Pentecostal bodies teach a separate work of sanctification. The Pentecostal Holiness Church (Articles of Faith, 10) calls it 'a definite, instantaneous work of grace achieved by faith subsequent to regeneration', and the Church of God, Cleveland (Declaration of Faith) lists 'sanctification subsequent to the new birth'.

title: Carry One Another, Boast in the Cross
sum: Paul turns to life together. If someone is overtaken by a wrong step, those who live by the Spirit should put that person back on his feet, gently (6:1). Believers are to carry each other's heavy loads and so fulfill 'the law of Christ' (6:2), while each person still carries his own pack (6:5). Students share with their teachers, and Paul reminds them that people harvest what they sow, and that they should not grow tired of doing good (6:6-10).

Then Paul takes the pen himself. In large letters he sums up the whole letter (6:11-18): the circumcision party wants a fine show in the flesh and an escape from persecution; Paul will boast only in the cross, through which the world is crucified to him and he to the world. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; a new creation is what matters. He blesses all who walk by this rule, and 'the Israel of God,' and ends by saying he bears the marks of Jesus in his body.
readings: Read as practical instruction for a church in conflict

Chapter 6 is not a list of unrelated tips. Each instruction answers the quarrel of 5:15 and 5:26: gentleness with the one who slips, shared burdens, honest testing of one's own work, support for teachers, patience in doing good.
Read as the letter's summary in Paul's own hand

In the ancient world the closing lines of a letter in the sender's hand gave its main point and its authority. 6:11-17 restates the letter in order: the false motive of the agitators, the cross as the only boast, the end of the circumcision distinction, the new creation, and Paul's body as the proof.

The last blessing, on 'all who walk by this rule' and 'the Israel of God' (6:16), has been read as a blessing of the church, of Jewish believers, or of the Jewish people. The way it is read says a good deal about how the reader thinks of the church and Israel; see the deep dive and the card.

views.H: The instructions of 6:1-10 suit an early assembly in a Roman city: a community with no formal law, no clergy as we know them, but with teachers who needed support (6:6), people liable to boast and compare (6:3-4), and slow, hard good works (6:9-10). The 'big letters' of 6:11 and the 'marks' of 6:17 belong to a world in which a letter's authority was shown by the sender's own hand, and in which slaves and devotees of a god might carry a brand. Paul's body bore the scars of beatings and stoning (2 Corinthians 11:23-25; Acts 14:19). Persecution (6:12) may have come from Jewish nationalist pressure or from local Jewish leaders, depending on who the agitators were.
views.C: The textual questions here are about 6:2 ('you will fulfill' or 'fulfill!'), 6:13 ('those who are being circumcised' or 'who have been'), 6:15 (the longer Byzantine form borrowed from 5:6), 6:17 ('Jesus' or 'the Lord Jesus') and the closing note 'written from Rome' that the Textus Receptus adds. The phrase 'the law of Christ' (6:2) has a close cousin only in 1 Corinthians 9:21 ('under Christ's law'), and the 'Israel of God' (6:16) appears nowhere else in the New Testament. In both cases the meaning must be argued from the context. Scholars also ask whether 6:11-18 is Paul's autograph subscription or a closing of the whole letter in his hand.
views.L: The chapter has two parts. The first (6:1-10) is a series of short commands tied to the harvest picture: sow and reap. The second (6:11-18) rings back to the start of the letter: Paul's opening claimed an apostleship 'not from men' (1:1), and here he ends with the marks of Jesus. The words 'boast' (6:13-14), 'flesh' (6:12-13), 'cross' (6:12, 14) and 'circumcision' (6:12-15) recur. The letter has no thanksgiving at the start and no personal greetings at the end; it closes with a blessing that echoes its opening 'grace and peace' (1:3). The final word before 'Amen' is 'brothers.'
views.J: The Jewish reader finds a letter that ends with a blessing on Israel, using a form of words (peace and mercy upon Israel) that echoes Jewish prayer. 'Walk by this rule' is halakhic language. 'New creation' was a Jewish hope, and Paul sets it above circumcision, which his Jewish contemporaries counted as the sign of the covenant. Whether 'the Israel of God' means the Jewish people, Jewish believers or the church is the central question of the Jewish reading (see the deep dive). The words 'new Israel' do not occur in Paul or anywhere else in the New Testament. The clearest early case of a Christian writer calling the church 'Israel' outright that this page can cite is Justin Martyr in the second century (Dialogue 11.5).
views.T: Luther's Galatians lectures (1535) take 6:16, 'peace be on them, and mercy', as the favor of God, the forgiveness of sins and peace of conscience for those who walk by the rule. Chrysostom took the 'marks' of 6:17 as Paul's wounds, which he bore like a soldier's. 'Peace upon the Israel of God' was read by Calvin as the church of Jews and Gentiles and by Chrysostom as those who keep the rule and follow grace; Nostra Aetate (1965) says the Jews 'should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God'. See the card.

deep.h: The Israel of God: how the words have been read
deep.b:
The Greek is kai epi ton Israel tou theou, 'and upon the Israel of God.' The clearest early case of a Christian writer calling the church 'Israel' outright that this page can cite is Justin Martyr, in the Dialogue with Trypho (about AD 160), who speaks of 'the true spiritual Israel' (Dialogue 11.5). Whether Galatians 6:16 is an earlier case is the very question here. Paul's own use elsewhere: 'Israel' is ethnic Israel (Romans 9:3-5; 11:1, 25-26; 1 Corinthians 10:18, 'Israel according to the flesh'), and he says 'not all who are from Israel are Israel' (Romans 9:6). If Galatians 6:16 were the church, it would be the one place where he uses it that way.

The grammar is open. Kai can be 'and also' (two groups: all who follow the rule, and Israel) or 'even' (one group). The order, 'peace upon them and mercy' and then 'upon the Israel of God,' does not settle it: both sides use it. The church of Jews and Gentiles was the view of Calvin, Chrysostom and Lightfoot, among others. Burton (1921) argued that the phrase means Jews, in particular the pious remnant of Israel, and gave two reasons: the order 'peace and mercy' reads oddly if both words belong to one group, and he found no place where Paul uses 'Israel' for anyone but the Jewish nation or part of it. After the Holocaust many churches re-examined whether the old reading helped to support the view that the church has replaced Israel. The Catholic Church (Nostra Aetate 4) says the Jews 'should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God'. Paul's own words in Romans 11:1 ("did God push his people away? By no means!") and Romans 11:29 are the usual test.

The Plain keeps 'and on the Israel of God' and lets the reader see the grammar.

Paul's body shows up at both ends of the argument's personal parts. In 4:13-15 he tells the Galatians that he came to them in a bodily weakness, that they did not spit at him, and that they would have given him their eyes. In 6:11-17 he writes in big letters (perhaps because of poor sight) and says he carries the marks of Jesus in his body. In between, the flesh of circumcision (6:12-13) is the thing the agitators want to boast about. The letter sets one flesh (circumcised, shown off) against another (scarred, suffering), and one boast (the Galatians' flesh) against another (the cross).

deep.title: Spec: the body of Paul as the letter's last argument
deep.b: Claude's theory, offered as a suggestion. Paul closes by pointing at himself: his handwriting, his scars, his weakness. I suggest that this is meant to match the opening of the personal appeal (4:13-15) and so to frame chapters 4-6 as a ring: the body that was weak and scorned, but welcomed by the Galatians, is the body that now bears the marks. The cross is what makes this readable. A crucified Messiah means the weak and scarred body is the proof of God's power, not its absence, and that is why Paul can say that circumcision, a mark of the flesh, counts for nothing. This overlaps with studies of the body in Galatians and with Gaventa's work on Paul as a parent; it would fail if 4:13-15 and 6:17 are unrelated and the scars come from a different cause than the illness of 4:13.

settings.to: The Galatian assemblies, with a word first to 'you who live by the Spirit'
settings.when: at the end of the letter, after the contrast of flesh and Spirit
settings.why: to show what the Spirit's fruit looks like in a community. A person who slips is to be mended, not cast out. Burdens are to be shared, but each person is responsible for his own work and for avoiding comparison. Support for teachers, perseverance in good work and kindness to all, above all the household of faith, close the section. The harvest image gives the warning: what you sow is what you reap.
settings.readers: A group of mostly Gentile believers, former pagans, who had been quarreling. The instructions apply the Spirit's fruit to concrete cases.

settings.what: Paul's postscript in his own hand
settings.to: The Galatian believers, in a final summary
settings.when: at the close of the letter, when Paul takes the pen from his scribe
settings.why: to restate the letter in a few lines and to give it his own authority. The agitators want a fine show in the flesh and escape from persecution; Paul boasts only in the cross. Circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing, a new creation is what matters, and he pronounces a blessing on all who follow this rule. His body, scarred by persecution, is his answer to anyone who would trouble him further.
settings.readers: A church that would hear the letter read aloud in a gathering. The last lines were heard as if Paul spoke them himself.
views: Written by a scribe, ending in Paul's hand
Paul dictated to a scribe and took the pen himself at 6:11 (the common view; compare Romans 16:22).
Paul wrote the whole letter himself, in large letters, because of his poor sight (some older readers).

traditions.q: Who is 'the Israel of God' (6:16), and does the church replace Israel?
views: Lumen Gentium 9 calls the people made up of Jew and Gentile 'the new People of God'. The Catechism quotes Paul that 'the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable' (839), and Nostra Aetate 4 says that although the Church is the new people of God, the Jews 'should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God'.

Chrysostom takes the Israel of God to be those who keep the rule, 'who desist from the old ways, and follow after grace'. People who descend from Israel but hold the opposite view, he says, have fallen away from 'both the relationship and the name itself'.
Calvin explained it as 'all believers, whether Jews or Gentiles, who were united into one church', the same people he called the children of Abraham by faith (3:29).

Charles Ryrie (Basic Theology, 1986, p. 399), as quoted at bible-researcher.com, takes 'the Israel of God' to be 'an especially important part' of the church, singled out for a special blessing. The same page lists Walvoord and S. Lewis Johnson with the reading that the phrase means Jewish believers.

The Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations says Messianic Judaism seeks 'to fulfill Israel's covenantal responsibility embodied in the Torah within a New Covenant context'. It calls the church 'the assembly of the faithful from the nations who are joined to Israel through the Messiah', so that Jews and Gentiles stay distinct yet are one community. The page does not comment on Galatians 6:16 itself.
